newsitem.title: USA: Tons of cocaine moved through Texas house - police.
newsitem.headline: Tons of cocaine moved through Texas house - police.

text.p: The Gulf Cartel drug smuggling operation moved several tonnes of cocaine a week through a safe house near the U.S.-Mexican border, police and a convicted drug trafficker said on Monday.

Sitting in a citrus grove three miles (4.8 km) from the border, a modest ranch house outside Harlingen, Texas, was equipped with an underground vault and was filled with more than nine tons (eight tonnes) of cocaine when it was raided in October 1989, Dagoberto Pena, a narcotics officer with the Texas Department of Public Safety, said.

Duffel bags, flour sacks and cardboard boxes stuffed with cocaine were found in the house, along with weapons, business ledgers and a confidential police report on an alleged cartel member, Pena said as testimony continued in Juan Garcia Abrego's trial on 22 counts of drug trafficking, money laundering and bribery.

Garcia Abrego, a 52-year-old former cookie factory employee from Texas, allegedly headed the Gulf Cartel. Arrested last January in Monterrey, Mexico, and flown to Houston for prosecution, he faces up to life in prison and the forfeiture of hundreds of millions of dollars in illicit drug proceeds if convicted.

During testimony on Monday, Alfonso Gonzalez Tristan, a labourer hired to drive and unload truckloads of cocaine and cash, said his job at the house was to "keep it clean, to help unload the money and the cocaine."
Ledgers found in the raid documented shipments of about 4,000 pounds (1,800 kg) moving through the house every few days, with packages identified by the source of the cocaine and its purity.
While U.S. drug agents were monitoring the smuggling operation through wiretaps and surveillance, the Gulf Cartel had ways of keeping tabs on federal investigations, Gonzalez told jurors.
At one point in 1989, he said, he was told to drive to McAllen, Texas, to pick up confidential police reports supplied to the organisation by an unnamed lawyer.

"They paid the lawyer to provide the reports," he said through a translator. One of the confidential reports, compiled by police on suspects in criminal cases, was found inside the house when it was raided.

The Gulf Cartel allegedly smuggled billions of dollars' worth of cocaine produced by Colombia's Cali cartel across the U.S.-Mexican border and was reputed to have moved up to a third of the cocaine consumed in the United States.

The biggest revelation in the trial's first week was that U.S. agents, despite more than three years of continous wiretapping of the cartel's phone conversations, had no recordings of Garcia Abrego or even the mention of his name on tape. The defence has hammered that point home at every opportunity.

There was little testimony about Garcia Abrego's alleged connections to Mexican government officials, although prosecutors said in opening arguments that the cartel paid out huge sums of money to buy protection and a former FBI agent testified that the drug empire was built on public corruption.

News reports have linked Garcia Abrego to Raul Salinas, the brother of former President Carlos Salinas, who is in jail in Mexico City on charges he ordered the 1994 assassination of a high ruling-party official.

Last week drug agents testified about the difficulties of maintaining wiretaps, because cartel insiders constantly changed phone numbers and residences as they shuffled money and cocaine between Mexico and the United States.

Moving into rented homes and apartments, the drug dealers would try to blend in to their surroundings. Witnesses told of a Houston house where the cartel members held a backyard barbecue in which guests sat outside drinking beer and watching their children play.
But while the meat smoked on the grill, several men put down their beers long enough to load 660 pounds (300 kg) of cocaine into a mobile home in the driveway.
